- **CAN-7USAT / VRITRA**: IN-SPACe CanSat competition 2026, Team 2026-INSPACe-CAN-7USAT-025, Lovely Professional University. ≤1000g, ≤150×400mm, dual-stage descent (drag chute + GPS-guided ram-air parafoil at 600m).
- **Teensy 4.1** (600MHz Cortex-M7): Primary flight MCU. Multiple hardware SPI buses (SPI0 and SPI1), hardware UART channels (Serial1 on pins 0/1), I2C (Wire on 18/19).

- **Semtech LR1121 (Core1121-XF)**: LoRa radio. Two distinct PA paths: HP (high-power, up to +22dBm) and LP. Must call `setOutputPower(N, true)` to force the HP PA pin. Has TCXO requiring `TCXO_V=1.6f`. RadioLib error code **-2 = RADIOLIB_ERR_CHIP_NOT_FOUND** means SPI communication is failing. RF parameters locked by competition: 867.00 MHz, SF10, BW125, CR4/5, sync word 0x98, preamble 8.

- **ESP32 gateway** (`esp32rec.ino`): Receives compact air frames, reassembles to a persistent 84-field record, injects RSSI/SNR/FREQ (only the receiver can know these), and emits full 84-field plain-decimal CSV over USB to the GCS PC. Also relays uplink commands from GCS into the CanSat's 600ms RX window.

- **DS3231 RTC**: Battery-backed real-time clock on I2C (addr 0x68). Provides mission clock continuity across Teensy resets. When combined with EEPROM persistence, `TIME_S` is computed as `rtc.now().unixtime() - missionBootEpoch` rather than `millis()/1000`, which resets to 0 on every reboot.

- **Quectel L89**: GPS+NavIC receiver. WAKE_UP/FORCE_ON hardwired to 3.3V in the physical build (always active, no GPIO control). RESET_N is active-low, idle HIGH, connected to Teensy D22. 1PPS not wired. Must NOT change baud rate (L89 doesn't persist PMTK251 changes to flash; always boots at 9600).

- **Subsystem independence principle**: Each hardware subsystem must be independently initializable; a failure in one must not stall or block the others. Radio init moved to earlier in `setup()` before the 5-second sensor calibration loops.

- I2C bus-sharing hazards: bus recovery (9 manual SCL pulses with SDA released) must run before every `Wire.begin()`, unconditionally, because all sensors share one physical bus and a wedge from an unrelated prior session/sketch can break the next boot's first transaction.

- Two-ray ground reflection RF propagation model and its breakpoint-distance dependence on antenna height — used to explain the gap between a ~400m bench-range result and the theoretical/achievable ~2km link budget.

But `threading.Thread` already has a **private method** called `_stop()` that CPython calls internally when finalizing a thread. Assigning `self._stop` overwrites that method with an `Event` object — so the next time internal thread bookkeeping (or your own `is_alive()` calls in `_update_chips`) tries to invoke it, you get `TypeError: 'Event' object is not callable`. That's exactly what's spamming your log and breaking the connect/status logic. Fixing this by renaming the attribute in all three classes.

- **CAN-7USAT / VRITRA**: IN-SPACe CanSat competition 2026, Team 2026-INSPACe-CAN-7USAT-025, Lovely Professional University. ≤1000g, ≤150×400mm, dual-stage descent (drag chute + GPS-guided ram-air parafoil at 600m).
- **Teensy 4.1** (600MHz Cortex-M7): Primary flight MCU. Multiple hardware SPI buses (SPI0 and SPI1), hardware UART channels (Serial1 on pins 0/1), I2C (Wire on 18/19).

- **Semtech LR1121 (Core1121-XF)**: LoRa radio. Two distinct PA paths: HP (high-power, up to +22dBm) and LP. Must call `setOutputPower(N, true)` to force the HP PA pin. Has TCXO requiring `TCXO_V=1.6f`. RadioLib error code **-2 = RADIOLIB_ERR_CHIP_NOT_FOUND** means SPI communication is failing. RF parameters locked by competition: 867.00 MHz, SF10, BW125, CR4/5, sync word 0x98, preamble 8.

- **ESP32 gateway** (`esp32rec.ino`): Receives compact air frames, reassembles to a persistent 84-field record, injects RSSI/SNR/FREQ (only the receiver can know these), and emits full 84-field plain-decimal CSV over USB to the GCS PC. Also relays uplink commands from GCS into the CanSat's 600ms RX window.

- **DS3231 RTC**: Battery-backed real-time clock on I2C (addr 0x68). Provides mission clock continuity across Teensy resets. When combined with EEPROM persistence, `TIME_S` is computed as `rtc.now().unixtime() - missionBootEpoch` rather than `millis()/1000`, which resets to 0 on every reboot.

- **Quectel L89**: GPS+NavIC receiver. WAKE_UP/FORCE_ON hardwired to 3.3V in the physical build (always active, no GPIO control). RESET_N is active-low, idle HIGH, connected to Teensy D22. 1PPS not wired. Must NOT change baud rate (L89 doesn't persist PMTK251 changes to flash; always boots at 9600).

- **Subsystem independence principle**: Each hardware subsystem must be independently initializable; a failure in one must not stall or block the others. Radio init moved to earlier in `setup()` before the 5-second sensor calibration loops.

Barometer** — there were **two** pad-reference variables that were never connected: `padPresPa` (persisted to EEPROM) and a file-scope `groundPressurePa` (what `getAltitudeAGL` actually read). `restoreCalibration()` wrote only the first, so **every reboot silently reverted the altitude datum to 101325 Pa** — at your 97.3 kPa pad that's ~340 m of error, and it's the direct cause of `ALTITUDE AGL −10.40 m` and `BARO VS GNSS ΔALT 263.70 m` in your screenshot. Also fixed: the 320 ms blocking `delay()` loop, averaging *raw* reads instead of median-filtered ones (one torn burst ≈ 1024 Pa ≈ 90 m, baking ~5.6 m of permanent offset), 20 ms sampling against a 40 ms sensor ODR, and the fixed `44330.8` constant — that's ISA-15 °C, and at your 28.9 °C the true scale height is 46469, so **every altitude read 4.8 % low**: ~48 m at 1000 m apogee, ~29 m at the 600 m deployment trigger that has a ±10 m tolerance.

Fixed with a `powerDirty_` flag retried at every idle pass.

I did not touch SF, BW, CR, sync or power. The real lever is antenna geometry:

- **The double-null at apogee is your worst case.** A whip has a deep null along its own axis. Your CanSat whip is axial (vertical under chute) and your ground whip is vertical — so when the vehicle is overhead near the pad, *each antenna's null points at the other*. **Tilt the ground antenna 30–45° toward the expected descent corridor.** This is the single biggest free gain and it costs nothing.
- **Height beats gain.** Every metre of ground-antenna elevation above clutter is worth more at 867 MHz than the omni→Yagi swap would give you at high elevation angles.
Shorter airtime doesn't raise the bitrate, but it lowers per-packet collision/fade exposure and buys cadence stability, which is the throughput you actually get to keep.

"Dual band" antennas sold with routers and access points are tuned for 2.4 GHz + 5 GHz WiFi, or 900 MHz + 1800 MHz cellular. Neither of those bands is 867 MHz. At 867 MHz that antenna is off-resonance, so most of the signal reflects back into the cable instead of radiating. The Friis equation treats TX and RX antenna gains symmetrically. Every dB of antenna efficiency is additive regardless of which end it sits on:
received power = TX power + TX antenna gain + path gain + RX antenna gain
So if the dual band antenna costs roughly 15 dB at 867 MHz (which is what the math suggests from your 30 dB two-antenna gap):
| TX antenna | RX antenna | RSSI vs best case |

The reason the two cases (dual band TX vs dual band RX) give identical results is **antenna reciprocity** — a passive antenna that radiates poorly at a given frequency also receives poorly at that same frequency, by the same amount. There is no way to "compensate" a weak TX antenna by putting a better antenna on the RX side more than you could do the reverse.
**Practical takeaway**: for your competition flight, run rubber ducky on both the CanSat and the ground station. Upgrading only one end still leaves you 15 dB short of where you could be.

## Short answer

You **cannot** rescue the dual band antenna to rubber-ducky level. The physics caps how much a matching network can recover, and 30 dB is far above that cap. But there is real optimisation available — roughly 6 to 12 dB — and it is all on the *rubber ducky path*, not the dual band one. None of it touches a single organiser-assigned parameter.

Your gap is 30 dB round trip, so ~15 dB per antenna. Reaching 15 dB from mismatch alone needs VSWR above 100:1 — essentially an open circuit. Real detuned whips sit at 5:1 to 15:1, which is 2.5 to 6 dB. **So most of your 30 dB is not reflection. It is radiation inefficiency.**

That distinction is the whole answer. A matching network fixes reflection. It cannot fix efficiency. If that antenna is physically a 2.4 GHz element (~31 mm radiator), at 867 MHz it is 0.09 λ — electrically short, radiation resistance around 1–2 Ω. Conjugate-matching it means forcing current through a loading coil whose own ohmic resistance is comparable to or larger than the radiation resistance, so most of your power heats the coil. The literature on electrically short monopoles is unanimous on this: matching networks adjust impedance but cannot recover losses inherent to low radiation resistance, and the network's own loss cannot be eliminated, only minimised.

"Dual band" antennas sold with routers and access points are tuned for 2.4 GHz + 5 GHz WiFi, or 900 MHz + 1800 MHz cellular. Neither of those bands is 867 MHz. At 867 MHz that antenna is off-resonance, so most of the signal reflects back into the cable instead of radiating. The Friis equation treats TX and RX antenna gains symmetrically. Every dB of antenna efficiency is additive regardless of which end it sits on:
received power = TX power + TX antenna gain + path gain + RX antenna gain
So if the dual band antenna costs roughly 15 dB at 867 MHz (which is what the math suggests from your 30 dB two-antenna gap):
| TX antenna | RX antenna | RSSI vs best case |

The reason the two cases (dual band TX vs dual band RX) give identical results is **antenna reciprocity** — a passive antenna that radiates poorly at a given frequency also receives poorly at that same frequency, by the same amount. There is no way to "compensate" a weak TX antenna by putting a better antenna on the RX side more than you could do the reverse.
**Practical takeaway**: for your competition flight, run rubber ducky on both the CanSat and the ground station. Upgrading only one end still leaves you 15 dB short of where you could be.

## Short answer

You **cannot** rescue the dual band antenna to rubber-ducky level. The physics caps how much a matching network can recover, and 30 dB is far above that cap. But there is real optimisation available — roughly 6 to 12 dB — and it is all on the *rubber ducky path*, not the dual band one. None of it touches a single organiser-assigned parameter.

Your gap is 30 dB round trip, so ~15 dB per antenna. Reaching 15 dB from mismatch alone needs VSWR above 100:1 — essentially an open circuit. Real detuned whips sit at 5:1 to 15:1, which is 2.5 to 6 dB. **So most of your 30 dB is not reflection. It is radiation inefficiency.**

That distinction is the whole answer. A matching network fixes reflection. It cannot fix efficiency. If that antenna is physically a 2.4 GHz element (~31 mm radiator), at 867 MHz it is 0.09 λ — electrically short, radiation resistance around 1–2 Ω. Conjugate-matching it means forcing current through a loading coil whose own ohmic resistance is comparable to or larger than the radiation resistance, so most of your power heats the coil. The literature on electrically short monopoles is unanimous on this: matching networks adjust impedance but cannot recover losses inherent to low radiation resistance, and the network's own loss cannot be eliminated, only minimised.

The Friis equation treats TX and RX antenna gains symmetrically. Every dB of antenna efficiency is additive regardless of which end it sits on:
received power = TX power + TX antenna gain + path gain + RX antenna gain
So if the dual band antenna costs roughly 15 dB at 867 MHz (which is what the math suggests from your 30 dB two-antenna gap):
| TX antenna | RX antenna | RSSI vs best case |

The reason the two cases (dual band TX vs dual band RX) give identical results is **antenna reciprocity** — a passive antenna that radiates poorly at a given frequency also receives poorly at that same frequency, by the same amount. There is no way to "compensate" a weak TX antenna by putting a better antenna on the RX side more than you could do the reverse.
**Practical takeaway**: for your competition flight, run rubber ducky on both the CanSat and the ground station. Upgrading only one end still leaves you 15 dB short of where you could be.

## Short answer

You **cannot** rescue the dual band antenna to rubber-ducky level. The physics caps how much a matching network can recover, and 30 dB is far above that cap. But there is real optimisation available — roughly 6 to 12 dB — and it is all on the *rubber ducky path*, not the dual band one. None of it touches a single organiser-assigned parameter.

Your gap is 30 dB round trip, so ~15 dB per antenna. Reaching 15 dB from mismatch alone needs VSWR above 100:1 — essentially an open circuit. Real detuned whips sit at 5:1 to 15:1, which is 2.5 to 6 dB. **So most of your 30 dB is not reflection. It is radiation inefficiency.**

That distinction is the whole answer. A matching network fixes reflection. It cannot fix efficiency. If that antenna is physically a 2.4 GHz element (~31 mm radiator), at 867 MHz it is 0.09 λ — electrically short, radiation resistance around 1–2 Ω. Conjugate-matching it means forcing current through a loading coil whose own ohmic resistance is comparable to or larger than the radiation resistance, so most of your power heats the coil. The literature on electrically short monopoles is unanimous on this: matching networks adjust impedance but cannot recover losses inherent to low radiation resistance, and the network's own loss cannot be eliminated, only minimised.

**No packet is ever sent twice.** `queueDownlink()` overwrites a single slot rather than queueing, so of the 10 packets built per second the radio sends 1 and discards 9. `PKT` and the rotation index both derive from `Radio.txCount()`, which only advances on a real transmission, so no packet number repeats. The uplink *does* repeat 6×, but `handleRxPacket()` de-duplicates on `<seq>`, so a command executes once. That part is clean.

`GsGnssLink` is a complete NMEA reader with an **ATTACH** button on the Recovery tab. But `_on_gs_fix()` feeds it only to the differential corrector — it never becomes "my position" and never reaches the map. That's why `ed_mypos` says *"paste lat, lon from your phone"*. `GroundTrack.mark()` exists and is **never called**, so there are no pins for you, the pad, or the target.

You'll need a GNSS source though — a laptop has no GPS. Either a USB dongle (u-blox VK-172 class, ~₹700) or your phone streaming NMEA over Bluetooth serial; both appear as a COM port and `GsGnssLink` handles them as-is.

Your pin numbering, by the way, is **fine** — I checked all nine symbol/footprint pairs including the 48-pad Teensy. That bug stayed fixed.
- **DS3231 deleted** — no mandatory field needs a battery-backed RTC. Field 2 is time-since-power-up (`millis()`); absolute time comes from GNSS. Also clears 0x68 and the 0x57 EEPROM off I²C.

- **UART mux deleted** — replaced by broadcasting the GNSS. L89 TX is one output and UART RX pins are inputs, so Boards 1, 3 and 5 can all listen permanently. Only Board 1 drives L89 RX, through 1 k. If Board 1 dies, the backup was already receiving. That removes a 35×23 mm module, 25 pads, the `MUX_SEL` net and a whole failover mode.

**On field 2 ("time since initial power"):** that field is satisfied by the Teensy's own `millis()` counter — no RTC needed, and it literally cannot fail as long as the Teensy is running. The real wall-clock datum the rules want is field 8, **GNSS TIME**, which comes from the L89, not a RTC. So DS3231 isn't load-bearing for any of the 16 mandatory fields. That said, you have a legitimate reason to want it anyway — timestamping SD log filenames before GNSS gets a fix — so I'm keeping it, just flagging that it's a convenience, not a rule requirement, so you don't spend fabrication risk defending it as one.

**On "logging must survive even if Teensy hangs":** a flash chip has no brain of its own — something has to drive its SPI bus to write to it. If Teensy hangs, nothing writes to *any* flash, no matter which physical board it sits on. The thing that actually gives you "logging happens no matter what" is already in your architecture: **Board 3 (backup) has its own independent microSD and takes over telemetry** when the watchdog confirms Primary is dead. That's the real answer to your requirement — not where the flash chip physically sits.

## 3. INA260 wiring (you have one)
Put it in the **battery position (U1)** on the POWER board, in series with the main battery line:
- Battery **+** → rocker switch → fuse → INA260 **IN+**.
- INA260 **IN−** → the VBAT bus, which feeds the ESC and the buck converters.

**Charging status:** a positive current means the pack is discharging. A negative current only appears if the charger connects on the IN− side. The INA260 can't see a charger clipped straight onto the battery leads.
The INA260 you already have is the better fit here.
- **Camera without the mux:** two short wires on Board 2's empty mux pads would connect MAIN straight to the camera:
You don't need the mux. Two short insulated wires across the empty mux footprint on **Board 2** connect the camera straight to MAIN, using the cable and copper already on your boards.
- **Radio off:** Wi-Fi and Bluetooth must be off (2.4 GHz rule).

You set this module to 9 V with a solder bridge on its back. But check your steering servos first.
- **IN +** goes to battery + (after the switch and INA260). **IN −** goes to GND.

**1. Your steering servos are 8 V parts.** The POWER board's M3 rail is meant to be **8 V** for the two A20CLM servos. This module can't make 8 V; it only offers 3.3, 5, 9 or 12 V. Check the maximum voltage printed on the servo or its datasheet:

**2. Your 3S battery is only "12 V" when full.** It reads 12.6 V when charged, about 11.1 V in the middle, and around 9–10 V near empty. A buck can't output more than its input, and it needs roughly 1 V of headroom. So the 9 V output **starts to sag once the battery falls below about 10 V**, which is about 3.3 V per cell. That's acceptable if you land before the battery is that low, but don't expect a steady 9 V down to empty.
Use the module's default 5 V (no pads bridged) for **M1** (5 V logic) and **M2** (5 V servo). This module has a 3.3 V pad, so it can also do **M4/M5**.
